articles.title: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues - Iran International
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia intercepts Houthi missiles, drones as Yemen fighting continues  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over Riyadh and southern parts of the country on Sunday as fighting with Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis continued, the Saudi-led coalition said.
The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched toward Riyadh, while a cruise missile targeted Khamis Mushait in the south. It later said 10 ballistic missiles aimed at southern Saudi Arabia had also been intercepted.
Saudi civil defense authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait before later saying the danger had passed.
Houthis threaten Riyadh airport
Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport remained a “military target” and warned airlines, airport staff and travelers against using it.
The airport resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after an October 10 attack, which the Houthis said they carried out, killed 13 people and wounded more than 300.
The Houthis also said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not directly confirm those assertions.
Fighting intensifies around Red Sea routes
Saudi Arabia has stepped up strikes against the Houthis after the group seized territory along Yemen’s Red Sea coast last month, bringing the fighting closer to the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a major global shipping route.
The renewed conflict has broken a UN-brokered truce that had largely held since 2022.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen’s civil war in 2015 at the head of a coalition backing the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized Sanaa the previous year.

articles.title: Houthi attacks rock Riyadh when Saudi Arabia reopens airport
articles.summary: Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued Sunday, rocking capital Riyadh as it prepared to reopen its international airport. Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting...
articles.full_text:
Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia continued Sunday, rocking capital Riyadh as it prepared to reopen its international airport.
Saudi Arabia, which leads a military coalition fighting the Iran-backed Houthis, has faced a barrage of strikes from the group in recent weeks.
The fighting erupted after a yearslong truce between the Houthis and Yemen's Riyadh-backed government fell apart.
Riyadh's international airport said flights would resume Sunday after a two-week closure following the Houthi strikes. However, it remained unclear to what extent the airport was operational.
The Houthi fighters have carried out waves of strikes on the airport, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.
The group has also targeted oil infrastructure and other sites, with the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen announcing Sunday it had intercepted 10 Houthi missiles fired at southern Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target."
"The Yemeni Armed Forces warn all international, regional and local airlines – as well as staff and travelers – against using King Khalid Airport in Riyadh, as it is unsafe and serves as a military target for our forces," he said.
"The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport."
An AFP journalist in the city heard three explosions in the early hours of Sunday, with residents receiving alert messages for a "hostile aerial threat" urging them to stay in a safe place.
The warning came as the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis said it had downed a ballistic missile launched by the group towards Riyadh, as well as two drones in the capital area.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched by the terrorist Houthi militia toward Riyadh," the coalition posted on X.
Later Sunday morning, the coalition said its forces intercepted a cruise missile fired by the Houthis at the kingdom's southern city of Khamis Mushait.
Attacks appeared to target areas across the south, with warnings also issued for Abha city and Namas Governorate.
"The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning – may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Khamis Mushait said Sunday on condition of anonymity.
The attacks came after the Houthi fighters said that – in the space of 24 hours – they targeted three Saudi airports, including in Riyadh, energy installations, a pipeline and an air base.
The Saudi civil defense agency said it had also responded to falling debris in the Mecca and Medina regions on Saturday after intercepting two Houthi missiles.
The Houthis denied targeting the cities, the two holiest in Islam, calling the Saudi claim a "huge lie."
The Houthis also fired at the southern Yemeni city of Aden, the interim seat of the Saudi-backed government, saying they targeted a naval base and military camp overseen by Saudi forces.
The flare-up in Yemen, with the Houthis taking control of the entire Red Sea coast in a lightning offensive last month, has further destabilized the region and disrupted oil markets.
The Houthi attacks have dealt a blow to Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest exporter of crude, disrupting businesses, airlines and residents, and rattling its drive to shift its international image.

articles.title: Iran unlikely to change position even if US, Israel resume war
articles.summary: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change Tehran’s position. The remarks come amid m...
articles.full_text:
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change Tehran’s position.
The remarks come amid mounting U.S. and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran, as U.S. President Donald Trump said Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the U.S.-Israeli campaign on Iran that began Feb. 28.
"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," Araghchi said during a televised event in Tehran.
"They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past."
An April 8 cease-fire between Iran and the U.S. ended the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.
These military flare-ups have subsided in recent weeks.
Iran has claimed control over the strait since the war began, regularly targeting vessels that attempt crossing without its authorization. Washington and countries in the region strongly oppose these moves.
In response, the U.S. maintains a naval counterblockade on Iranian ports.
In June, Iran agreed with the U.S. to a memorandum of understanding outlining a path to permanent conflict settlement, but the deal later unraveled as each side accused the other of violating it.
Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.
"The current war has changed everything. We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same," Araghchi said.
"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

articles.title: Major Israeli preelection ops in West Bank displace thousands
articles.summary: The Israeli military pressed ahead with a major operation in the occupied West Bank Sunday, displacing thousands of Palestinians and restricting movement following a Friday attack...
articles.full_text:
The Israeli military pressed ahead with a major operation in the occupied West Bank Sunday, displacing thousands of Palestinians and restricting movement following a Friday attack in Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers and wounded three.
The operation comes as Israel enters the final days before a tense election, which is largely seen as a referendum on current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s leadership and security policies during the past three years of war.
Most Palestinian workers with permits will not be allowed to enter Israeli settlements for work in the occupied West Bank Sunday and Monday, and crossings into Israel will remain closed until after Israel’s elections Tuesday, the Israeli military said.
The military said it operated in more than 400 different locations over the weekend and arrested 40 Palestinians it claimed were affiliated with Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad. It said the operation is continuing at the same intensity Sunday.
The Hebron municipality said the operation displaced more than 2,200 people, including nearly 300 children under the age of 18.
The military said that troops were conducting searches in the area where the gunmen operated and warned residents to evacuate Deir Bahha, the suspected gunmen’s neighborhood.
After Friday’s attack, Israel’s military claimed it found weapons in the gunmen’s car and that they were allegedly planning to attack Israeli civilians before being stopped at the checkpoint.
All entrances and exits to the city remained sealed, with the epicenter of the operation in Deir Bahha and another part of the city called al-Jalda, according to Hebron Mayor Yousef Zuhair al-Jabari.
"People cannot reach or enter the city, and they cannot leave it. The blockade has affected every aspect of life," al-Jabari said. He added that the blockade is forcing businesses to close and has also shuttered a mosque.
"The army told us that this area would be closed for 12 days. Now they’re saying 12 days, but maybe they’ll leave the area after two or three days," said Shadi al-Qawasmi, a Hebron resident who was displaced with his family. "This may be because of the elections or some political matter no one knows except God Almighty."
The operation forced some families to navigate crossings on foot in order to leave Hebron after the roads were closed to traffic. At some military gates, people passed sacks of flour and gas canisters through the gates, while an elderly man pushed his wife in a wheelchair through an opening beside one of them. Another family attempted to navigate the gate to access medical appointments.
Hebron municipal officials said families had been displaced from nearly 500 apartments in Deir Bahha and surrounding neighborhoods.
In the West Bank, which is experiencing a surge of Israeli violence, 112 Palestinians have been killed this year, according to the Ramallah-based Palestinian Health Ministry. During the same period, Six Israelis have been killed.
The latest attack sparked outrage in Israel, with Netanyahu and three members of his right-wing government giving statements from the site of the attack Friday afternoon, vowing to respond forcefully.
"We warned a few weeks ago about attempts by our enemies to harm us, our citizens and our soldiers ahead of the election," Netanyahu, trying to bolster his image ahead of the election, said. "We will act to destroy this place."
Roughly 3 million Palestinians and 540,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank, which Israel occupied in the 1967 Mideast war.
Hebron is one of its most tense cities and the only place where Jewish extremist settlers live in the heart of a densely populated Palestinian area under Israeli military protection.

articles.title: Over 400,000 march across France in serious challenge to Macron
articles.summary: Clashes broke out in Paris Saturday following nationwide protests that drew more than 400,000 people over school funding and rising living costs, leading to nearly 1,000 arrests in...
articles.full_text:
Clashes broke out in Paris Saturday following nationwide protests that drew more than 400,000 people over school funding and rising living costs, leading to nearly 1,000 arrests in a fresh challenge to President Emmanuel Macron.
The Paris march began peacefully, a week after widespread rioting and looting during protests across the country. But near the demonstration's endpoint in eastern Paris, masked protesters hurled objects and fireworks at police, who answered with clouds of tear gas, deafening sound grenades and jets of water cannons.
Officers with megaphones urged protesters to disperse. Some demonstrators panicked as tear-gas canisters landed in their midst, scattering with screams. Veteran protesters shouted after them: "Don’t run!"
The Interior Ministry put nationwide turnout at 410,000 – fewer than the 550,000 it said protested last weekend – while the CGT union that helped organize some of Saturday's protests estimated nearly 800,000.
The ministry’s estimate included 110,000 in Paris, where authorities confined the march to the city’s southeastern edge, away from the center. The CGT put the number of protesters in Paris at 250,000.
More than a month of unrest that started with protests in high schools for more funding and teachers is testing Macron’s authority in the final months of his presidency before voters choose his successor in May.
The stakes are high: The far-right National Rally party has accused his government of failing to protect the public and urged people to channel their anger into votes for its candidate Marine Le Pen.
On the far left, presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon has backed demonstrators and criticized policing that has left some teenage protesters with life-changing injuries.
As dusk fell Saturday, violence erupted at the end of some of the 289 protests counted by the Interior Ministry nationwide. Street fires burned in the cities of Marseille and Lyon.
Police used tear gas in Lyon, Clermont–Ferrand, Strasbourg and Bordeaux and water cannons in Nice and Nantes, French media reported. In Nice, far-right extremists fought with demonstrators downtown and 11 people were arrested, regional authorities said.
Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said police made nearly 1,000 arrests but added that the number is expected to increase significantly as more are counted.
Nunez said beefed-up policing, with 70,000 officers backed by helicopters, armored vehicles and other support, helped prevent a repeat of widespread looting and damage to shops the previous weekend.
What began last month as a protest over staff shortages at one high school southeast of Paris spread nationwide, drawing students demanding more funding for education and workers seeking help with soaring costs for fuel and other necessities.
In Paris, Benedicte Pittion, a 46–year–old teacher, marched with her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, a high school student – in their first protest together.
"The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them," Pittion said.
Garance said she'd been "really scared" after seeing the previous weekend’s violence, but felt that staying away would hand the government a victory.
Macron met high school representatives Friday. They said he had promised to overhaul university admissions, but they called for protests to continue until concrete measures are announced.
Soumaya Abed, a 58-year-old nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, complained that authorities in Paris wanted to stifle protesters by making them march on the capital's outskirts, keeping them away from the center where the Louvre and other major museums closed exceptionally.
"But it won’t stop the movement. It won’t stop students from demanding better conditions in schools," she said.
Other protesters expressed anger about record poverty and wealth inequality under Macron. Camille Chesnier, 27, said she hasn't found work despite having an engineering degree and a master’s degree.
"There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren’t privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it’s very tough," she said."
In Marseille, police put attendance at 17,000, while the CGT union estimated 100,000. In the southwestern city of Toulouse, 26,500 people joined the protests, according to authorities. Authorities had banned rallies in cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier.
Trade unions criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
Thousands also marched Saturday in Orleans, south of Paris, in a separate peaceful protest against the far right as Le Pen’s National Rally held a two-day congress in the city.
Gendarmes stood guard Saturday beneath the Arc de Triomphe and shopkeepers boarded up storefronts across Paris. Near the Saint-Lazare train station Saturday, Akram Ahmed, a 34–year–old contractor, was boarding up an optician’s shop.
"I got the call last night," he said. "The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life."
Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Student groups want 250,000 more places in higher education and an end to selection through Parcoursup, the national admissions system.
Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
They are also seeking help with everyday costs: an extra 200 euros ($224) a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing.
Energy prices in France were 21.3% higher in September than a year earlier, helping drive overall inflation to 3.1%, according to the national statistics agency, INSEE.
Paris protester Louis Ledoux-Xatard voiced frustration over inequality.
"Looking at countries like the United States, we don’t want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing," he said.
"I never imagined that I’d be taking to the streets so much before my thirties."
